sourceFacts.claim: Initial BindAsync obtains the configuration loader's reload token only when reload-on-change is enabled and hosting-address preference does not override configured endpoints, then registers TriggerRebind. That callback invokes RebindAsync. RebindAsync acquires the same _bindSemaphore used for binding/shutdown, checks _stopping, obtains the next token, calls Reload, and only calls StopEndpointsAsync when endpointsToStop.Count is positive. Its finally block rearms the callback and releases the semaphore. A token notification alone need not produce a nonempty stop list.
sourceFacts.boundary: Selected exact caller bodies establish this static producer chain, not a repository-wide caller census or executed server behavior.

sourceFacts.claim: Reload copies the prior ConfigurationBackedListenOptions to a fresh endpointsToStop list. It builds a new ConfigurationReader, processes the new endpoints, removes value-equal reusable old options from that stop list, and records newly configured options separately. It updates ConfigurationBackedListenOptions only after endpoint processing. The server then copies each remaining old ListenOptions.EndpointConfig reference into a new List<EndpointConfig> of the exact old-stop count. The target does not receive arbitrary expanded endpoint lists from this caller.

ConfigurationReader materializes one EndpointConfig per item returned by IConfiguration.GetSection("Endpoints").GetChildren(), reads its URL, SNI/configuration and other settings, and caches that reader's resulting list. The selected producer has no numeric endpoint cap or list-size clamp. That is not evidence that a particular production application has many endpoints. For an ordinary successful generation, the stop-list size is bounded by the previous configuration-backed logical listen-options count, not by an invented benchmark parameter.
sourceFacts.unknown: Actual application endpoint counts, custom IConfiguration provider behavior, natural changed/removed fractions and production reload frequency.

sourceFacts.claim: A successful transport bind selects the first supporting factory and starts one accepting listener, which adds an ActiveTransport containing the passed EndpointConfig reference. It does not add one ActiveTransport per request or connection, or one for every registered factory. The server can bind stream and multiplexed protocols for the same listen option. AddressBinder can select LocalhostListenOptions, whose IPv4 and IPv6 clones preserve the exact EndpointConfig reference, yielding multiple real active transports for one logical configured endpoint when those binds succeed.
sourceFacts.limit: These are concrete multiplicity mechanisms, not a universal transport-count bound. Failure residue and unread custom/HTTPS/transport implementations prevent that inference.

sourceFacts.claim: Options maintains separate code-backed and configuration-backed lists and snapshots them together for binding. Its normal Listen(EndPoint, Action) producer constructs ListenOptions without an EndpointConfig, applies defaults/callback and adds it to the code-backed list; null-config active transports are skipped before Contains. Configure(IConfiguration, bool) documents that reload updates only Endpoints-section endpoints, not code-defined endpoints. The one-argument Configure overload passes reloadOnChange:false, but that overload alone does not establish hosting defaults. Loader.GetReloadToken combines the configuration token with an optional certificate-watch token. Unchanged/reused endpoints and no-op notifications can avoid target invocation even while reload handling itself runs.
sourceFacts.unknown: Hosting setup/default registration, provider event coalescing, actual certificate/configuration change cadence and how often those changes remove or modify endpoints.

sourceFacts.claim: KestrelServerImpl.StopAsync first establishes stopping, cancels _stopCts, waits for the bind semaphore, and calls TransportManager.StopAsync. The latter copies _transports directly into StopTransportsAsync. It does not call StopEndpointsAsync or run endpointsToStop.Contains. Dispose delegates to StopAsync with a canceled token. A repeated full-shutdown workload would therefore characterize the wrong selection path.

The target iterates all _transports, short-circuits null EndpointConfig, and tests list membership using EndpointConfig value equality. EndpointConfig is sealed and overrides Equals/GetHashCode: name, URL, normalized protocol/TLS/client-certificate defaults, certificate, SNI dictionaries and a cloned configuration-section snapshot participate. Equality is not reference identity, name-only identity or URL-only identity. ConfigSectionClone recursively compares children; its hash uses the value and child count, allowing collisions without making unequal snapshots equivalent.

transportsToStop preserves the original active-transport traversal order and includes each matching ActiveTransport entry once. Repeating an equal stop-list item cannot itself add the same transport twice, while several distinct real listeners sharing one configuration must all remain selected. The reader does not explicitly deduplicate GetChildren results; no universal uniqueness promise is inferred for arbitrary configuration providers. A membership index must not become the output enumerator or collapse active listeners by configuration.

The manager's active list lives with the server; the real caller's stop list is fresh and local to one rebind, and selection completes synchronously before StopTransportsAsync's asynchronous work. The bind semaphore serializes the selected bind/rebind/shutdown owners. EndpointConfig nevertheless has mutable protocol/certificate fields and a mutable SNI dictionary. The live IConfigurationSection is snapshotted for equality because configuration changes. CertificateConfig.FileHasChanged participates in equality and hashing, and CertificatePathWatcher really sets it under its separate metadata lock before raising its reload token. Reload updates certificate watches, including removal of stopped endpoint certificates, before it returns.
sourceFacts.notClaimed: A mutable field alone does not prove a race during target selection. Full stopped-key hash stability across default-certificate/HTTPS aliasing has not been proved within the selected inputs; the watcher-removal ordering must not be ignored.

sourceFacts.claim: Selection itself does not observe cancellation. Its caller creates a token linked to shutdown and schedules cancellation after five seconds before invoking the target; this is not a preemptive bound on synchronous list scanning. StopTransportsAsync starts unbinds, awaits them all, closes connections with abort fallback, disposes listeners, then removes selected entries from _transports. Failure before final removal can leave entries present. Rebind catches/logs failure and rearms its token in finally; ordinary shutdown propagates failure through _stoppedTcs. Preserve this sequencing and the synchronous-selection/asynchronous-stop boundary.

Let T be all active-transport entries, C the entries with nonnull EndpointConfig, and S the real stop-list count. This selection performs T outer checks and up to C*S value-membership comparisons, whose cost is not necessarily a primitive comparison. It is not simply request volume times endpoint count. A transient hash index would add construction, hashing and storage and would retain collision/equality costs; no crossover is established. Other selected code still scans old endpoints for reuse, calls RemoveAll, and removes stopped transports individually from a List. Improving this one membership seam would not prove linear whole-reload complexity or improved end-to-end reload latency.
sourceFacts.materiality: Unknown, neither measured beneficial nor measured no-gain. Reconfiguration lifecycle is a workload boundary, not a rejection reason.
